lesson.title: Follow the food

steps.headline: In a food web, each arrow points from the food to the organism that eats it.

lead.text: A food web shows who eats whom. Algae → zooplankton means that zooplankton eat algae.
A producer, such as algae or grass, makes its own food. A consumer eats other organisms.

steps.headline: How many direct food sources does the heron have in this pond web?

workedSteps.text: Find the arrows that end at the heron.
Small fish → heron, and zooplankton → heron.
Follow each route back. Both start at algae.

steps.headline: How many direct food sources does the hawk have in this meadow web?

workedSteps.text: Find the arrows that end at the hawk.

steps.headline: Matter is recycled in an ecosystem. Energy flows through it and disperses.

lead.text: Decomposers return matter from dead material to the soil and water, where producers can use it again.
Energy is not recycled. Most of it disperses as heat, so an ecosystem needs a steady input, usually light.
Every route in a web starts somewhere. Look for the organism that does not need to eat anything.

reveal.text: You found the start of every route. Everything else in the pond depends on the algae, directly or through other consumers.

lead.text: A small web shows who eats whom. Imagine the number of mice falling and ask what you could say about the hawks.

reveal.text: Arrows show feeding links and say nothing about numbers. Predicting a count needs more than a small diagram.

lesson.orientation: Read feeding arrows and separate energy flow from recycled matter.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A pond has algae, tiny animals called zooplankton that eat the algae, and small fish that eat the zooplankton.
A disease kills most of the zooplankton.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a food web's arrows and say which parts of an ecosystem are recycled and which are not.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you predict what a change to one species does to the rest of a habitat.

recap.keyIdea: Arrows point from food to eater, and every route starts at a producer. Matter is recycled by decomposers, but energy flows through and disperses as heat.

blocks.text: You counted direct food sources for a heron and a hawk. You traced routes back to the producer and said why a diagram cannot predict a count.

recap.nextHook: Energy thins out along every route. How much reaches the top?

questions.prompt: What does the arrow Grass → Grasshopper mean?
hints: Follow the direction of matter and energy transfer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Arrows run from food to consumer.

choices.label: Grass turns directly into a hawk

questions.onCorrect: The grasshopper eats the grass. An arrow runs from the food to the eater.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the arrow backwards. It points to whichever organism is doing the eating.
An arrow shows eating, not turning into another organism.

questions.prompt: A pond web has algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron. Which of these is the producer?
hints: Which organism makes its own food from light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Algae build organic matter using light; the other organisms consume other organisms.

questions.onCorrect: Algae. They build their own food, so all the other organisms depend on them.

misconceptions.feedback: Animals eat other organisms. The producer is the one that makes its own food.

questions.prompt: In a meadow web, a hawk eats mice and frogs. Frogs eat grasshoppers, which eat grass. How many direct food sources does the hawk have?
hints: Count the arrows ending at the hawk.
Do not count indirect food sources.
Ignore the grass and the grasshopper: the hawk does not eat them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two arrows enter the hawk: one from mouse and one from frog.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Count only the arrows that end at the hawk.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every organism in the web. Count only those the hawk eats directly.
That includes organisms further down the routes. Count only direct links.

questions.prompt: Energy flows through ecosystems and becomes less available for further biological work. In what form does much of it disperse?
hints: Think about metabolic energy that is not passed into new biomass.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy disperses as heat; atoms can be recycled through environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Heat. Energy flows through and spreads out as heat, so ecosystems need a steady input.

misconceptions.feedback: Atoms are recycled. Energy is not, and it spreads out in another form.

questions.prompt: The number of mice decreases. Can a small food web diagram give an exact future hawk count?
hints: Check what the arrows actually show.

acceptedIdeas: No, other food sources and conditions also matter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A feeding web shows relationships, not a complete quantitative population model.

choices.label: Yes, arrows specify exact population changes
No, other food sources and conditions also matter

questions.onCorrect: No. Arrows show who eats whom, not how many. Other food and conditions matter too.

misconceptions.feedback: Arrows show feeding links only. They give no numbers.
The hawk also eats frogs, so losing mice does not remove its food entirely.

questions.prompt: A pond web is a chain of algae, zooplankton, small fish and a heron, plus one extra link where the heron also eats zooplankton directly. How many feeding links does the web have in total?
hints: Count the links in the chain first.
A chain of four organisms has one fewer link than organisms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The chain has 3 links, and the extra link makes 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Count the links in the chain, then add the shortcut.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chain alone. Add the extra link.
That is one more than the web has. A chain of four organisms has three links.

questions.prompt: In a food web an arrow points from a rabbit to a fox. Which organism is the consumer?
hints: Which way does an arrow point?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The arrow runs from food to consumer, so the fox eats the rabbit.

questions.onCorrect: The fox. The arrow points to the eater.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow starts at the food. The rabbit is being eaten here.

questions.prompt: Which kind of organism returns matter from dead material to the soil and water so that producers can use it again?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Decomposers return matter from dead material to environmental pools.

questions.onCorrect: Decomposers. They recycle matter, though energy is not recycled with it.

misconceptions.feedback: Producers use the recycled matter. Another group returns it.

questions.prompt: What happens to the amount of algae at first?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With fewer zooplankton eating it, the algae increases at first.

questions.onCorrect: It increases. Fewer eaters mean less algae is eaten, which is how links in a web connect.

misconceptions.feedback: The algae's eaters were killed. Less of it is being eaten, not more.

questions.prompt: Why do all the routes in a web trace back to a producer?
hints: Where does the first food in the web come from?

acceptedIdeas: Producers are the only organisms that make their own food, so every other organism depends on them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only producers make their own food, so every consumer's energy traces back to them.

choices.label: Producers are the only organisms that make their own food, so every other organism depends on them
Producers are always the largest organisms
Producers eat all the other organisms

questions.onCorrect: Producers make their own food. Every consumer's energy comes from them, directly or not.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide it. Grass and algae are producers because they make their own food.
Producers are not eaters. The arrows run from them to the consumers.
